mean: to take the blame to protect others

mean: a third party profiting from a quarrel

story.text: The state of Zhao was about to attack Yan. Su Dai, sent by Yan, told the King of Zhao: a clam opened its shell to sun itself and a snipe pecked at it, so the clam snapped shut on the bird's beak. Neither would let go, each sure the other would die first, and a passing fisherman caught them both. If Zhao and Yan wear each other out, he said, Qin will be that fisherman. The king called off the attack.
story.source: Zhan Guo Ce (戦国策), Strategies of Yan

lit: the force of splitting bamboo: once the first joints give, the whole stalk splits by itself

mean: to call a halt to a plan
lit: to call out 'wait!' and stop the play

story.text: The phrase comes from the call 'matta!' (wait!). In sumo, a wrestler who is not ready can hold back at the initial charge and the start is redone; in shogi and go, a player who regrets a move asks for a 'matta' to take it back. From this call that stops play, the phrase came to mean stepping in to halt any plan already under way.

ctx.en: The doctor put a stop to my father's plan to run the marathon.

ctx.s: マンションの建設[けんせつ]は、住民[じゅうみん]の反対[はんたい]で{待[ま]ったがかかった}。
ctx.en: Construction of the apartment block was halted by residents' opposition.

ctx.s: 合併[がっぺい]の話[はなし]は順調[じゅんちょう]だったが、当局[とうきょく]が{待[ま]ったをかけ}、手続[てつづ]きは止[と]まった。
ctx.en: The merger was going smoothly, but the authorities stepped in and the process was halted.

bad.s: 駅[えき]で友達[ともだち]を三十分[さんじゅっぷん]も{待[ま]ったをかけた}。
bad.en: (meant: I kept my friend waiting at the station for half an hour)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with waiting for someone. Keeping a person waiting is mataseta.

bad.s: 疲[つか]れたので、自分[じぶん]の勉強[べんきょう]に{待[ま]ったをかけて}寝[ね]た。
bad.en: (meant: I was tired, so I paused my studying and went to bed)
bad.why: It is stepping in to stop someone else's plan, not pausing your own activity. Say benkyo o chudan shite.

lit: the skin of one's mug is thick: nothing makes them blush

use.how: Predicate (面の皮が厚い) or before a noun (面の皮の厚い人). A blunt insult for someone who does shameless things without a trace of embarrassment.

near.diff: 図々しい is the everyday adjective for pushy or cheeky; 面の皮が厚い is a rougher, more cutting idiom for utter shamelessness.

cue: A neighbour who never returned your lawnmower knocks again to borrow your car, smiling as if nothing had happened.

ctx.s: 借[か]りた金[かね]も返[かえ]さずにまた頼[たの]みに来[く]るなんて、{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]い}。
ctx.en: Coming back to ask again without repaying what he borrowed? The nerve of him.

ctx.s: 「人[ひと]の手柄[てがら]を自分[じぶん]のものにするなんて、本当[ほんとう]に{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]い}ね。」
ctx.en: "Taking credit for someone else's work? You're really shameless."

ctx.s: 列[れつ]に平気[へいき]で割[わ]り込[こ]むとは、{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]い}にもほどがある。
ctx.en: Cutting into the queue without a second thought? That's shameless beyond belief.

ctx.s: 招待[しょうたい]もされていないのに料理[りょうり]を持[も]ち帰[かえ]るなんて、{面[つら]の皮[かわ]の厚[あつ]い}人[ひと]だ。
ctx.en: Taking food home from a party he wasn't even invited to? What a brazen man.

ctx.s: 遅刻[ちこく]してきたのに一番[いちばん]いい席[せき]に座[すわ]るとは、彼[かれ]も{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]い}。
ctx.en: Turning up late and then taking the best seat? He's got some nerve.

ctx.s: 「よく平気[へいき]な顔[かお]でそんな嘘[うそ]がつけるね。{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]すぎる}よ。」
ctx.en: "How can you tell a lie like that with a straight face? You're utterly shameless."

bad.s: 冬[ふゆ]は乾燥[かんそう]して、{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]く}なった。
bad.en: (meant: the dry winter made my facial skin rough)
bad.why: It is only figurative, about shamelessness. Rough facial skin is hada ga areta.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{面[つら]の皮[かわ]が厚[あつ]い}から、大勢[おおぜい]の前[まえ]でも堂々[どうどう]と発表[はっぴょう]できて素晴[すば]らしい。
bad.en: (meant: she's admirably unflappable and presents confidently in front of crowds)
bad.why: It is an insult, never praise for confidence. Admirable composure is dokyo ga aru or mono-oji shinai.
